subhead: Local SEO for Devon — more calls, more bookings, more customers.
meta: SEO company in Devon: county-wide SEO for Exeter, Plymouth, Torbay and rural Devon — tourism, hospitality, trades and B2B. Free audit.
intro: As an SEO company serving Devon, I help businesses turn Google into their best salesperson — across a county, not a city. Devon is four distinct economies: Exeter's year-round professional market, Plymouth's naval and marine supply chain, Torbay's seasonal visitor economy, and rural Devon's villages. You work directly with me, a specialist doing SEO since 2019: one real page per real market, seasonal content timed to rank, no thin town pages.

why.heading: Devon is a county, not a city — your SEO has to act like it.
why.body: Devon's £1.6bn visitor economy supports 50,000+ jobs; farming is a bedrock sector with ~30% of the UK's dairy industry; Brixham lands one of the country's most valuable catches. But the county is four distinct markets: Exeter (year-round professional, highest competition), Plymouth (naval/marine B2B, thin competition), Torbay (sharply seasonal tourism), and rural/coastal Devon (village-specific, low competition, high intent). Targeting 'Devon' as one market is the most common mistake — the winners own their patch with town-specific pages and seasonal content.

section1.heading: The multi-location playbook that actually works in Devon.
section1.body: One 'areas we cover' page listing fifty towns ranks for nothing. The playbook: one substantial page per real market (Exeter, Plymouth, Torquay, Barnstaple, Exmouth, South Hams…), each with genuine local proof; one Google Business Profile per genuine location with honest service areas; a county hub page linking to town spokes for topical authority; Devon-specific citations; and reviews that name the place. Single-location businesses should own their patch completely before expanding — depth beats breadth.

section2.heading: Devon's seasonal search calendar.
section2.body: Content needs 6-10 weeks to rank, so every seasonal push starts before the season. Jan-Mar: planners booking summer — holiday lets and wedding venues publish now. Apr-Jun: 'things to do in Devon' season switches on. Jul-Aug: 'near me' everything from visitors' phones — profiles must be flawless. Sep-Dec: Christmas and winter breaks, then build for next year. Publishing summer content in June is already too late — the rankings were decided in March. SEO in Devon is a calendar discipline.

facts: Devon's visitor economy is worth £1.6 billion a year and supports over 50,000 jobs — around 9% of all employment in the county — with a Local Visitor Economy Partnership accreditation backing its growth.
Exeter is Devon's county city: home to the University of Exeter, Exeter Science Park's tech cluster, the Met Office and Pennon Group — and the professional-services hub for the whole of rural Devon.
Plymouth hosts HMNB Devonport, the largest naval base in Western Europe, anchoring a marine, defence and engineering supply chain across the city.
Torbay — Torquay, Paignton and Brixham — is the English Riviera, one of Britain's most popular seaside destinations, with an economy built on tourism, hospitality and holiday lets.
Brixham is one of the UK's most productive fishing ports by value of catch, and Devon is home to around 30% of the UK's dairy industry — farming and fishing remain bedrock sectors.
Devon's business base is overwhelmingly small and micro businesses, which makes the county's economy resilient — and means most local firms are doing their own marketing on top of everything else.

faqs.q: I have branches in Exeter and Torquay — do I need a page for each?
faqs.a: Yes — and each one needs to earn its place. A thin 'Exeter' page and a thin 'Torquay' page will both underperform; what works is a substantial page per location with genuine local proof (local photos, local testimonials, location-specific services and access notes), linked from a county hub page. That structure builds topical authority for 'Devon' terms while each page fights its local battle. One generic page trying to cover both cities ranks for neither.

faqs.q: How do I get bookings in winter when tourism searches collapse?
faqs.a: You plan for it in autumn. Winter content — off-season breaks, locals' offers, Christmas and New Year packages in Torquay, winter wedding deals — needs to be live by October to rank for December searches. And keep your review engine running through the quiet months: winter guests' reviews keep your profile looking alive to February bookers planning summer trips. The businesses that go dark in November spend March catching up.

faqs.q: Can one Google Business Profile cover the whole of Devon?
faqs.a: One profile with honest service areas can cover a service-area business, yes — but a profile for every town you don't genuinely operate from will get you suspended. The honest playbook: one profile per real location, service areas set truthfully, and win with reviews, photos and town-specific website content rather than fake pins. For single-location businesses, own your patch completely before expanding — depth beats breadth.

faqs.q: We're a farm shop in the South Hams — is SEO worth it for a rural business?
faqs.a: It's some of the best-value SEO in the county. Village-specific searches like 'farm shop South Hams' have low volume but extremely high intent, and almost no rural businesses do SEO properly — so a rebuilt Google profile, a few genuine local pages and a steady review flow can dominate your patch within months. Low competition plus high-intent buyers is exactly where a small budget goes furthest.

faqs.q: Should I target 'Devon' keywords or specific towns like Barnstaple and Exmouth?
faqs.a: Specific towns first, 'Devon' second. Town terms ('wedding venue Barnstaple', 'plumber Exmouth') have lower competition, clearer intent and faster wins — and they're what your customers actually type. Build town pages with real local proof, link them from a county hub page, and the 'Devon' authority follows naturally. Targeting 'Devon' generically from day one is the most common mistake I see: it reads as being about nothing in particular, and Google treats it that way.
